source.title: Data coarse graining can improve model performance.
source.authors: Alex Nguyen; David J. Schwab; Wave Ngampruetikorn

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes a linear-regression double-descent curve and refines its interpretation by showing that optimal regularization removes that peak while a separate risk nonmonotonicity can remain.
record.gate_note: The study also reports risk curves while varying coarse-graining schemes. Those results concern coarse-graining level, not model size, training epochs, or sample size; the optimally regularized scheme comparisons are recorded under fits_no_version. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study's own analytical risk landscapes and simulations for ridge or min-norm linear regression show a peak at the interpolation threshold qγ = 1. This includes a sample-varying path and feature-count paths that cross the threshold. Under optimal ridge tuning the peak vanishes. These results reproduce known linear-regression theory (Hastie et al.; Nakkiran et al. 2021) in a new coarse-graining setting. They are not a refutation of any version, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that high-pass coarse graining can lower risk by trading signal fidelity against estimator variance. They argue that optimal regularization shows this nonmonotonicity is distinct from double descent, whose interpolation-threshold peak it suppresses.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an analytical and simulated high-dimensional ridge-linear-regression model, rather than the deep-network settings and sweeps associated with the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk depends on the coarse-graining scheme and level, the parameter-to-sample ratio, and regularization; optimal regularization removes the interpolation-threshold peak.

fits_no_version.finding: With optimal ridge tuning, high-pass coarse graining keeps a nonmonotonic risk curve with an intermediate minimum. Low-pass and random-pass coarse graining give monotonically increasing risk.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing low-signal features can lower prediction risk, independently of double descent, through a tradeoff between misspecification bias and variance.

record.problems: The analysis assumes isotropic features and a linear-regression model; the authors identify extensions to more complex data and nonlinear models as future work. Several plotted results are described qualitatively rather than reported as numerical risk values.

untested.parts: No deep networks and no model-size sweep of neural networks.
Deep-network settings; only asymptotic linear ridge regression is analysed.
Only linear regression, with no other model classes compared. Whether the second descent beats the classical minimum is not assessed.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epochs and samples.
The role of label noise or variance in driving the peak is not varied (snr fixed at 4). Multiple or triple descent is not examined.
No re-expression against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Feature-count (q) sweep across the interpolation threshold in ridgeless regression, including the random-pass scheme (η = q). It shows risk divergence at qγ = 1 and descent on the over-parameterized side. Theory matches simulations with N = 1200 and P = 1200 or 1600.
Ridgeless analytic risk formula (Eq. 28), giving the divergence at qγ = 1 in closed form, which bears on V3's sample-path peak

record.verdict_notes: Double-descent results here are reproductions of known asymptotic linear-regression theory (Hastie et al. 2022; Nakkiran et al. 2021), used as a contrast to the coarse-graining effect. Treat them as weak, setting-specific confirmations. They are not independent empirical tests on deep networks. Fig. 2 panels use ridgeless min-norm regression; Figs 3-4 use λ = 0.01 and optimal λ respectively.

versions.untested_parts: Training epochs or training time are not swept.
The sample-size result is for the study's theoretical linear-regression setting, not deep networks.
The study does not test capacity growth past interpolation across model classes.
It does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and samples.
It tests the disappearance of the double-descent peak under optimally tuned ridge regularization. It does not test whether label noise drives the peak or whether multiple peaks can occur.
It does not re-express the second descent using an effective parameter count to test whether it becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: ridge-regularized linear regression
rows.operation_detail: Vary the sample count, and thus the parameter-to-sample ratio, with all features retained.

conditions.value: λ = 0.01 in Fig. 3; the accompanying limiting analysis takes λ → 0+

rows.measure: Average prediction risk as sample count varies
rows.value: The risk landscape has a maximum at the interpolation threshold qγ = 1; the sample-varying path exhibits standard double-descent behavior. The text identifies the path toward that threshold as accessible by adding more data.
rows.note: The text and plot describe the peak, rather than providing a numerical risk value for each sample count. This supports the more-data-can-hurt result on the over-parameterized side as increasing sample count approaches the interpolation threshold.
rows.check: Evidence is a heatmap plus text, with no per-sample risk numbers. The result is purely theoretical, from Eqs (15), (21), (23), (24) with λ = 0.01 and snr = 4. Adding data moves γ from 1.5 toward 1, into the high-risk ridge. Eq. (28) gives the ridgeless form.

rows.subject: ridge-regularized linear regression
rows.operation_detail: Vary the effective parameter-to-sample ratio along the sample-varying path while tuning ridge regularization to minimize prediction risk.

conditions.value: optimally tuned; λ* given by Eq. (29)
snr = 4 for the Fig. 3 comparison; other parameters as in Fig. 3

rows.measure: Prediction-risk curve around the interpolation threshold
rows.baseline: Fig. 3 uses λ = 0.01 and shows a double-descent ridge at qγ = 1.
rows.value: Under optimal regularization, the double-descent ridge at qγ = 1 is entirely absent.
rows.note: This records the study's stated result for the sample-varying double-descent path under optimally tuned ridge regularization.
rows.check: Bears only on the 'disappears under optimally tuned regularization' part of V6. Eq. (29) defines the optimal λ per point. The text says the ridge is 'entirely absent'.

rows.subject: ridge-regularized linear regression
rows.operation_detail: Vary the degree of high-pass coarse graining, preferentially removing low-signal features.
rows.value: Risk is nonmonotonic, with a minimum at an intermediate coarse-graining level.
rows.note: This is a risk curve against coarse-graining level, not one of the axes named in V1–V7.
rows.check: Risk versus coarse-graining level under optimal ridge; this axis is not one named by any version. Correctly unlinked.

rows.subject: ridge-regularized linear regression
rows.operation_detail: Vary the degree of low-pass coarse graining, preferentially removing high-signal features.
rows.note: The stated monotonic increase is not a fall-rise-fall double-descent curve; it is included as a contrasting coarse-graining result.
rows.check: Monotonic risk increase versus coarse-graining level under optimal ridge; not a double-descent axis. Correctly unlinked.

rows.subject: ridge-regularized linear regression
rows.operation_detail: Vary the degree of random-pass coarse graining, removing features without preferential selection by signal.
rows.note: The stated monotonic increase is not a fall-rise-fall double-descent curve; it is included as a contrasting coarse-graining result.
rows.check: Monotonic risk increase versus coarse-graining level under optimal ridge; not a double-descent axis. Correctly unlinked.

relationships.condition: Asymptotic ridge linear regression, all features kept, γ = 1.5, snr = 4, λ = 0.01 (theory)
relationships.reason: On the sample path in Fig. 3, adding data moves toward qγ = 1, where the risk ridge peaks (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Adding data along the studied sample path moved toward the risk peak at qγ = 1.

relationships.condition: Asymptotic linear regression with optimally tuned ridge λ* (Eq. 29)
relationships.reason: The text says the double-descent ridge at qγ = 1 is 'entirely absent' under optimal tuning (R2).
relationships.display_finding: Optimal ridge tuning entirely removed the double-descent peak at qγ=1.

relationships.condition: Min-norm linear regression, γ = 1.33 and 1.5, random-pass feature removal (theory plus simulations, N = 1200)
relationships.reason: Based on text and Fig. 2c-d, not a row. Risk diverges as feature count crosses qγ = 1 and falls on the over-parameterized side.
relationships.display_finding: Risk diverged as the feature sweep crossed qγ = 1 and declined on the overparameterized side.
